q: High-risk prostate cancer is best identified by combining:
o: PSA, biopsy grade and clinical stage (plus extent of cancer on biopsy)
e: At least 10% of new diagnoses are locally advanced. Risk tools are most accurate in low-risk disease and tend to overestimate recurrence in high-risk disease.

q: Neoadjuvant ADT before radical prostatectomy:
o: Reduces positive margin rates but does not improve PSA-free survival
e: In one study margins fell from about 50% to 15%. Four randomised trials showed no reduction in biochemical failure, so it has no routine role before surgery.
s: Ch 159 Locally advanced prostate cancer; Ch 161

q: Among men having prostatectomy for clinical T3 disease, how many turn out to have organ-confined disease (overstaging)?
e: So selected cT3 men can still be good surgical candidates.

q: High-dose bicalutamide (150 mg) monotherapy:
o: Reduced progression in locally advanced disease but increased mortality in localised disease (HR about 1.23)
Has no effect on sexual function
e: Avoid it in low-risk localised disease.

q: For high-risk or locally advanced disease treated with EBRT, the best-supported ADT schedule is:
o: Neoadjuvant plus concurrent plus adjuvant ADT, with longer courses giving better outcomes
e: RTOG and EORTC trials favour long-term ADT, usually 18–36 months. Longer ADT increases sexual dysfunction and possibly rectal toxicity.

q: EORTC 22911 and SWOG 8794 showed that adjuvant radiotherapy for pT3 disease after prostatectomy improved:
o: Biochemical and local control, and in SWOG 8794 metastasis-free and overall survival; most benefit with positive margins
e: RADICALS-RT, RAVES and GETUG-AFU 17 (2020) later showed early salvage radiotherapy is as good as adjuvant, so observation with early salvage is now preferred for most men.

q: Typical radiotherapy dose to the prostate bed after prostatectomy:
e: ASTRO and AUA recommend a minimum of 64 Gy for salvage. Higher doses (up to about 76 Gy) have been explored.
s: Ch 159 Locally advanced prostate cancer; Ch 160

q: Lymph node metastases found at radical prostatectomy (completed): the trial showing a survival gain with immediate ADT is:
o: Messing ECOG 3886 (all men had the prostatectomy)
e: In EORTC 30846, where the prostatectomy was abandoned, immediate ADT gave no survival benefit. Radiotherapy plus ADT may be best for pN1.
s: Ch 159 Locally advanced prostate cancer; Ch 161

q: Which finding after prostatectomy predicts progression despite adjuvant local therapy?
o: Seminal vesicle invasion or positive nodes
e: In the Kattan postoperative nomogram, a high preoperative PSA (for example 17) contributes strongly to recurrence risk.

q: Over the decade covered by CaPSURE, how has treatment of high-risk (CAPRA 6–10) disease changed?
o: Less primary ADT and more radical prostatectomy
e: The rates of surveillance and watchful waiting stayed stable.

q: Four years after prostatectomy for pT3a Gleason 8, PSA has risen slowly to 1.2, and CT shows a mass beside the anastomosis in front of the rectum. Most likely:
o: Local recurrence in the prostatectomy bed
e: PSMA PET or MRI would now be the preferred imaging.

q: The AUA/EAU definition of biochemical recurrence after radical prostatectomy is:
o: PSA 0.2 ng/mL or more, confirmed by a second value
e: After radiotherapy, Phoenix failure is the nadir plus 2 ng/mL.

q: Per this chapter, the most sensitive imaging for local recurrence at low PSA after prostatectomy is mpMRI. Today the preferred test is:
e: The chapter quotes MRI sensitivity up to 86% at PSA 0.4–1.4. PSMA PET detects recurrence even below 0.5 ng/mL and is now guideline-preferred. CT and bone scan add little below a PSA of 10.

q: Which is NOT required before salvage prostatectomy after radiotherapy?
o: Separate negative pelvic lymph node sampling
Life expectancy of at least 10 years
e: Ideally the PSA is below 10. Frozen-section nodes at surgery are reasonable but not mandatory.

q: The most sensitive imaging for local recurrence after radiotherapy (per chapter) is:
e: TRUS is no better than DRE, and CT is of no use at PSA below 20. A biopsy after radiotherapy can be interpreted about 30 months after treatment.

q: The best approach to a rising PSA after definitive local therapy is:
o: Stratify by Gleason score, PSA doubling time, time to recurrence and competing mortality, then match the treatment
e: Biochemical recurrence after surgery often progresses slowly. The median time to bone metastases is about 10 years.

q: Which statement about salvage radiotherapy is correct?
o: Offer it to men with non-metastatic rising PSA after prostatectomy, and consider ADT with it, especially for high-risk features
e: RTOG 9601 (bicalutamide) and GETUG-AFU 16 support adding ADT to salvage radiotherapy.

q: Which is NOT a recognised side effect of ADT?
e: Others include anaemia, cognitive change, sarcopenia, diabetes and cardiovascular risk.

q: A transient rise in PSA after local therapy should prompt:
o: Close monitoring, because not all men progress to biochemical or clinical failure
e: After brachytherapy, PSA bounces are common.

q: Oestrogens (such as DES) work in prostate cancer mainly by:
e: Oestradiol suppresses LH and FSH about 1000 times more potently than testosterone. Aminoglutethimide blocks the cholesterol-to-pregnenolone step.

q: Starting a non-steroidal antiandrogen (bicalutamide or flutamide) as monotherapy causes:
o: LH, testosterone and oestrogen all fall
LH, testosterone and oestrogen all rise
e: Central feedback is blocked. The extra testosterone is converted to oestrogen, causing gynaecomastia and breast pain. Steroidal cyproterone instead lowers LH.

q: Which side-effect pairing is correct?
o: Nilutamide: delayed dark adaptation (about 25%) and interstitial pneumonitis (about 1%)
e: Flutamide causes diarrhoea. All non-steroidal antiandrogens can cause liver toxicity, so check liver function. Cyproterone causes fluid retention and thromboembolism.

q: LHRH agonists lower testosterone by:
o: Desensitising pituitary LHRH receptors after continuous exposure (after an initial flare)
e: The flare lasts 10–20 days. Give an antiandrogen at the same time and continue it for about 3 weeks. They are modified at amino-acid position 6 for potency, and survival equals orchidectomy.

q: How quickly does bilateral orchidectomy lower testosterone?
e: When tying the cord, use double ligation including one transfixion suture.

q: Which predicts a POOR response to ADT?
o: Long PSA doubling time before ADT
PSA still detectable on ADT (about 15-fold higher odds of castration resistance at 24 months)
e: Higher Gleason score also predicts earlier castration resistance.

q: Which statement on ADT side effects is correct?
o: About 1 in 5 men keep some sexual activity, but only about 1 in 20 keep a strong libido
e: The average man becomes osteopenic within about 4 years. Hot flushes affect 50–80%. Radiotherapy (10 Gy) prevents gynaecomastia only if given before it starts.

q: Bothersome hot flushes on ADT can be treated with:
o: Megestrol, medroxyprogesterone, cyproterone, low-dose oestrogen or gabapentin
e: Treat hot flushes only if they bother the patient.

q: Combined androgen blockade (LHRH agonist plus antiandrogen):
o: Is the same as secondary hormone therapy
Aims to block adrenal androgens; gives a small survival gain with non-steroidal agents, but slightly worse outcomes with cyproterone
e: Adding flutamide to orchidectomy gave no significant benefit in minimal metastatic disease (the NCI trial).

q: Early ADT, compared with deferred ADT, before metastases appear:
o: Does not prevent castration resistance, and in low-risk localised disease increases overall mortality
Improves survival in all disease states
Is needed for every rise in PSA
e: Many men never need ADT because the disease progresses slowly.

q: In the PR.7 trial (intermittent vs continuous ADT for rising PSA after radiotherapy):
o: Intermittent ADT was better for survival
Off-treatment intervals shortened with each cycle (20 to 13 to 9 months) and quality of life improved; overall survival was non-inferior
e: There were more prostate-cancer deaths in the intermittent arm and more deaths from other causes in the continuous arm.

q: Which form of ADT is the cheapest?
e: Combined androgen blockade is the most expensive. An LHRH agonist is cheaper than orchidectomy only if the patient lives a few months.

q: ADT is always indicated in a hormonally intact man with:
e: ADT is not indicated for high-grade PIN. For metastatic hormone-sensitive disease, ADT is now intensified with an ARPI and/or docetaxel (LATITUDE, TITAN, ARCHES, ARASENS).

q: Which steroid synthesis inhibitor needs both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement?
e: Abiraterone needs prednisone because it causes mineralocorticoid excess (hypertension, hypokalaemia, fluid retention).

q: Why is ADT continued after a man becomes castration-resistant?
o: Because the androgen receptor stays active and responsive even at castrate testosterone levels
e: Mechanisms include receptor amplification, mutations, splice variants and androgen production within the tumour. Castration-resistant is not the same as hormone-insensitive.

q: Stopping a non-steroidal antiandrogen in a man on combined blockade whose PSA is rising can:
o: Produce a PSA decline (antiandrogen withdrawal response) because antiandrogens can act as agonists
e: Mutant androgen receptors can be stimulated by the antiandrogen itself.

q: About what proportion of men with metastatic prostate cancer die of other causes?
e: This is why weighing competing risks matters even in advanced disease.

q: Compared with LHRH agonists, LHRH (GnRH) antagonists:
o: Lower LH and testosterone at once without a flare; the early antagonist abarelix was limited by severe allergic reactions
e: Degarelix (injection) and relugolix (oral; HERO trial) are current antagonists. All agonists are given by injection or implant.

q: Castrate-level testosterone is defined as below:
e: Most modern assays and LHRH analogues achieve below 20 ng/dL. Castration resistance needs PSA or radiographic progression despite castrate testosterone.

q: Docetaxel for mCRPC:
o: Is given every 3 weeks with prednisone, and improved survival and quality of life vs mitoxantrone (TAX 327)
Should be stopped if PSA rises during the first 3 cycles
e: Do not stop it for an early PSA rise (flare). Side effects: neutropenia, fatigue, neuropathy, watery eyes and nail changes.

q: Cabazitaxel (TROPIC trial):
o: Improved survival vs mitoxantrone after docetaxel; more neutropenic fever and diarrhoea, less neuropathy
e: CARD (2019) later showed cabazitaxel beats a second ARPI after docetaxel plus one ARPI.

q: Abiraterone acts by:
o: CYP17 (17α-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase) inhibition, blocking adrenal and tumour androgen synthesis; given with prednisone
e: Watch for hypertension, hypokalaemia, oedema and liver toxicity. It improved survival before docetaxel (COU-AA-302) and after it (COU-AA-301).

q: Compared with bicalutamide, enzalutamide:
o: Has higher androgen receptor affinity and also blocks nuclear translocation and DNA binding
e: Survival benefit in AFFIRM (after docetaxel) and PREVAIL (before docetaxel). Seizure risk is a recognised side effect.

q: A man with known bone metastases develops new back pain. Correct management:
o: Rely on a stable bone scan
Suspect cord or root compression: high-dose dexamethasone, urgent whole-spine MRI, then radiotherapy or surgical decompression
e: If he is not already on ADT, orchidectomy (or ketoconazole with steroids) gives rapid castration.

q: A man with rapidly progressing visceral disease and low PSA on ADT should have:
o: A biopsy to look for neuroendocrine or small-cell transformation; if confirmed, platinum-based chemotherapy
e: These tumours are AR-negative, PSA-negative and stain for neuroendocrine markers, and often spread to viscera and brain.

q: Which statement about radium-223 is FALSE?
o: It is an alpha emitter with a range under 100 μm
It is approved only after docetaxel
e: It is approved for symptomatic bone-predominant mCRPC without visceral metastases, with or without prior docetaxel. Do not combine it with abiraterone (ERA 223 showed more fractures).

q: Sipuleucel-T:
o: Is an autologous cell vaccine (antigen-presenting cells primed with PAP–GM-CSF) for asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic mCRPC; improved overall survival without changing PSA or progression-free survival
e: It was approved on overall survival (IMPACT trial). Monitoring PSA does not show whether it is working.

q: Which drug is NOT approved for non-metastatic (M0) CRPC?
e: The 2020 review names only apalutamide and enzalutamide. Darolutamide was also approved in 2019. All three improved metastasis-free and overall survival.

q: Skeletal-related events in mCRPC are reduced with:
o: Zoledronic acid or denosumab, with calcium and vitamin D
e: Check dental health first because of the risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw. Prostate bone metastases are usually sclerotic, so hypercalcaemia is rare.

q: A PSA doubling time below which value predicts a rapid clinical course in CRPC?
e: PSA is a poor marker of drug benefit, so progression-free survival is the better trial end point. Circulating tumour cells are being studied as a marker.

q: Beta-emitting bone-seeking agents (strontium-89, samarium-153) differ from radium-223 because they:
o: Cause more bone marrow suppression and give pain relief only, without a proven survival gain
e: Alpha particles are about 7000 times heavier than beta particles, and one or two hits can kill a cell.
